title: And that single sentence, buried inside a pastoral letter written nearly two thousand years ago, confronts one of the most painful misunderstandings still circulating in Christian communities today.
paragraphs: And that single sentence, buried inside a pastoral letter written nearly two thousand years ago, confronts one of the most painful misunderstandings still circulating in Christian communities today.
What happens when you love Jesus with everything you have, but your body still hurts?
What happens when you've prayed, fasted, believed, waited, and asked God for healing, yet tomorrow morning you wake up facing the same struggle?
Does that mean God has abandoned you?
Does it mean your faith is defective?
Or have we sometimes confused trusting God with refusing the very means through which He may provide help?
Before you answer, listen carefully to what Paul actually wrote.
In 1 Timothy 5:23, the King James Version records these words:
"Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities."
That is the verse.
No thunder.
No dramatic healing service.
No accusation.
Just an apostle giving personal, practical counsel to a beloved younger brother whose body was experiencing recurring difficulties.
But beneath those few words is a lesson about faith, suffering, wisdom, and the character of God that many believers have never fully considered.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying guilt that Jesus never asked them to carry.
The original Greek makes Paul's instruction especially interesting.
The verse begins:
Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει, ἀλλὰ οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ χρῶ
Transliterated:
Mēketi hydropotei, alla oinō oligō chrō.
A careful translation is:
"Do not continue drinking only water, but make use of a little wine."
The word μηκέτι (mēketi) means "no longer" or "not anymore."
The verb ὑδροπότει (hydropotei) concerns drinking water. In this context, the contrast suggests that Timothy had been drinking water without wine, and Paul advised him to change that practice.
Then comes οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ (oinō oligō).
"A little wine."
Not unlimited wine.
Not an invitation to intoxication.
Not permission to escape suffering through drunkenness.
A little wine.
The word χρῶ (chrō) comes from a verb meaning "to use" or "make use of."
Paul was recommending a limited, practical use of wine for Timothy's physical condition.
And then the apostle explains why.
διὰ τὸν στόμαχον καὶ τὰς πυκνάς σου ἀσθενείας
Dia ton stomachon kai tas pyknas sou astheneias.
"Because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses."
The Greek word στόμαχον (stomachon) refers to the stomach.
πυκνάς (pyknas) conveys the idea of frequent or recurring occurrences.
And ἀσθενείας (astheneias) refers to weaknesses, illnesses, or infirmities.
Paul was not addressing a single moment of discomfort.
He was referring to a pattern of physical trouble.
Timothy had recurring health problems.

Scripture does not identify the precise medical diagnosis. It does not tell us whether the problem involved digestion, contaminated water, chronic illness, or something else. Historical suggestions about wine's possible usefulness do not establish exactly why Paul recommended it.
What Scripture does establish is that Paul recognized Timothy's condition and recommended a modest practical measure.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible is not giving every Christian with stomach problems a universal prescription to drink alcohol.
It is preserving a particular instruction from Paul to Timothy.
We should neither erase that instruction nor turn it into something Paul never intended.
And now comes the question that changes the conversation.
Why didn't Paul simply tell Timothy to pray for healing?
Think about who was writing this letter.
This was the apostle Paul.
The man through whom God performed extraordinary miracles, as recorded in Acts 19:11–12.
The man who saw a crippled man healed in Lystra through the power of God, as described in Acts 14:8–10.
The man who prayed for Publius's sick father on Malta, laid hands on him, and saw him healed in Acts 28:8.
Paul believed in divine healing.
He had witnessed it.
He had participated in it.
He knew that Jesus Christ was not powerless over sickness.
And yet, when writing to Timothy, he recommended a practical response to recurring illness.
Why?
The text does not explicitly tell us why Paul chose this instruction rather than mentioning prayer.
We cannot responsibly conclude that Paul never prayed for Timothy, that Timothy never prayed for himself, or that God had refused to heal him.
Scripture simply does not reveal those details.
But the instruction does reveal something important.
Paul did not treat practical care for the body as a betrayal of faith.
Read that again.
The same apostle who trusted God for miracles could also recommend an ordinary physical measure.
For Paul, dependence on God and responsible action were not enemies.
They belonged in the same life.
And that should make us reconsider the way we sometimes speak to suffering Christians.
Because somewhere tonight, there is a mother who has prayed for healing while quietly wondering whether taking medication means she doesn't trust Jesus enough.
There is a father who has hidden his diagnosis because someone told him that speaking about sickness is making a negative confession.
There is a young believer who has been told that if healing hasn't come, there must be something wrong with their faith.
There is a faithful Christian sitting in a hospital waiting room, exhausted from fighting a battle they never asked to fight, silently wondering whether God is disappointed in them.
And there are people who love Jesus deeply but have begun to feel ashamed of needing help.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Needing medical care does not automatically mean you lack faith.
Taking prescribed medicine is not inherently a denial of God's power.
Seeking a qualified physician is not an act of spiritual surrender to unbelief.
And continuing to suffer does not, by itself, prove that you are living outside God's will.
Timothy's recurring infirmities did not cause Paul to dismiss him as spiritually useless.
Paul continued to entrust him with ministry.
He continued to instruct him.
He continued to love him.
The young man had physical weaknesses, but those weaknesses did not cancel his calling.
Perhaps that is the first burden someone needs to lay down today.
You have been treating your suffering as evidence that God has rejected you.
But Timothy's story gives you no reason to make that assumption.
There is another detail in this passage that deserves attention.
Immediately before Paul's instruction about wine, he wrote:
"Neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure." — 1 Timothy 5:22, KJV
Then comes verse 23, with its instruction about Timothy's stomach and frequent illnesses.
Then Paul continues discussing sins that become evident and good works that eventually come to light.
This means the wine instruction appears inside a larger discussion of church leadership, purity, discernment, and responsibility.

Some interpreters suggest that Timothy's practice of drinking only water may have reflected personal abstinence or religious caution. That is possible, but the text does not explicitly tell us his motive.
What we can say is that Paul did not want Timothy's physical needs neglected.
And that observation leads to a question worth asking.
Have you ever become so determined to appear spiritually strong that you stopped admitting you were physically, mentally, or emotionally exhausted?
You tell everyone, "I'm blessed."
But you haven't slept properly in weeks.
You tell your family, "God is in control."
And He is.
But you refuse to ask for help because you're afraid someone will think your faith is weak.
You smile at church.
You encourage other people.
You quote Scripture.
You pray for everyone else.
And then you return home, close the door, and quietly fall apart.
Not because you stopped loving Jesus.
But because you are human.
And human beings have limits.
Timothy did.
Paul did.
Even the greatest servants of God were never promised bodies that would never experience weakness.
The Bible does not command us to pretend otherwise.
In fact, Scripture repeatedly shows God's servants facing physical and emotional limitations.
Consider Elijah.
In 1 Kings 19, after an extraordinary confrontation with the prophets of Baal, Elijah fled in fear and became deeply distressed.
He sat beneath a broom tree and asked God to take his life.
What happened next?
God did not begin by delivering a lecture about Elijah's inadequate faith.
An angel provided food and water.
Elijah slept.
Then he ate again.
Only afterward did the account move toward the next stages of God's dealings with him.
Elijah needed spiritual direction, yes.
But he also needed nourishment and rest.
And God did not despise those needs.
Consider Epaphroditus.
In Philippians 2:25–27, Paul describes a fellow worker who became so sick that he nearly died.
Paul says God had mercy on him.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not accuse Epaphroditus of being spiritually defective.
He honors him.
He calls him a brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier.
His sickness did not erase his faithfulness.
Then consider Trophimus.
In 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul writes:
Stop there.
Paul left someone sick.
The apostle who witnessed extraordinary healings did not record an immediate healing for every sick person connected to his ministry.
We are not told why Trophimus remained sick at that moment.
We are not told whether he later recovered.
We are simply told that he was left sick.
That fact alone should make us cautious about condemning believers whose healing has not yet come.
And then there is Paul himself.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, Paul describes a "thorn in the flesh."
Christians have debated its exact nature for centuries. The passage does not clearly identify it as a particular physical disease, so we should not pretend otherwise.
But we do know that Paul pleaded with the Lord three times for it to depart.
And the Lord answered:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Paul asked for relief.
God answered with sustaining grace.
That does not mean every sickness must remain.
It does not mean we should stop praying for healing.
It means that God's faithfulness cannot be measured only by whether our circumstances change immediately.
Sometimes God grants healing in ways that astonish us.
Sometimes recovery comes through ordinary treatment and the body's natural processes.
Sometimes the struggle continues longer than we hoped.
And sometimes, despite our prayers and every available effort, suffering remains.
In every circumstance, Christians are called to trust the character of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
But here is where we must be careful.
We should never use Paul's instruction to Timothy to dismiss the power of prayer.
James 5:14–15 teaches believers to call for the elders of the church when they are sick and to pray in faith.
Prayer matters.
God hears His people.
We are invited to bring our needs before Him.
Yet the same Scriptures also show that practical action has a place.
In Luke 10:34, the Samaritan cares for a wounded man by binding his wounds and applying oil and wine.
In Colossians 4:14, Paul refers to Luke as "the beloved physician."
The Bible does not present the existence of physicians or physical care as inherently opposed to devotion to God.
We can pray while receiving treatment.
We can trust Christ while consulting a doctor.
We can ask God for healing while following sound medical advice.
These are not necessarily contradictory acts.
The danger begins when we turn faith into a test that Scripture itself has not established.
When someone says, "If you really believed, you wouldn't need medicine," they are placing a burden on suffering people that 1 Timothy 5:23 does not support.

When someone says, "Your illness proves you have hidden sin," they are ignoring passages such as John 9:1–3, where Jesus rejects the disciples' assumption that a man's blindness must have resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
And when someone says, "A faithful Christian will always be healed immediately," they are claiming more than the New Testament promises about the present life.
Jesus is still Lord.
God is still able to heal.
But we are not authorized to explain every person's illness by accusing them of unbelief.
Now consider something even more personal.
Why do we find it so difficult to admit weakness?
Perhaps because we have built an image of Christianity in which faithful people must always look victorious.
Always smiling.
Always energetic.
Always confident.
Always healthy.
Always financially stable.
Always emotionally composed.
But that is not the full picture of biblical discipleship.
The Christian life includes joy, peace, courage, and hope.
It also includes tears.
It includes endurance.
It includes waiting.
It includes dependence.
It includes moments when the strongest prayer you can manage is simply:
"Lord, help me."
And He is not offended by that prayer.
Think of the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
What a painfully human confession.
Faith and struggle in the same sentence.
Belief and weakness in the same breath.
And Jesus did not demand that the father manufacture an impressive spiritual performance before receiving help.
This is one reason the Gospel is such good news.
Jesus did not come merely to congratulate people who had successfully made themselves strong.
He came to save sinners.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to reconcile us to God through His death and resurrection.
And the grace that saves us is not something we earn by pretending we have no struggles.
It is received through faith in Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
Our salvation does not rest on a perfect medical record.
It does not rest on never feeling afraid.
It does not rest on proving that we can survive without help.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His grace.
And this is where Timothy's seemingly small instruction becomes unexpectedly beautiful.
Paul was concerned about Timothy's stomach.
Not merely his sermons.
Not merely his leadership.
Not merely his doctrinal accuracy.
His stomach.
His recurring illnesses.
His ordinary human vulnerability.
There is something deeply compassionate about that.
Paul could address the responsibilities of church leadership and still make room for the physical well-being of the person carrying those responsibilities.
That is not a distraction from discipleship.
It is part of loving a real human being.
And perhaps we need more of that in the Church today.
More believers who will pray with the sick without blaming them.
More pastors who will encourage appropriate medical care without treating it as spiritual compromise.
More Christian communities where someone can admit, "I'm struggling," without fearing judgment.
More compassion.
More truth.
More patience.
More Christlike love.
Because sometimes the person sitting beside you in church is fighting a battle you cannot see.
They may have spent the previous night in pain.
They may be waiting for test results.
They may be exhausted from treatment.
They may be caring for a sick child or an aging parent.
They may have prayed for months, perhaps years, and still have questions they are afraid to ask out loud.
And the last thing they need is someone casually declaring that their suffering proves their faith is inadequate.
They need the truth.
They need prayer.
They need wise care.
They need the love of Christ expressed through His people.
And sometimes, like Timothy, they need someone who cares enough to say:
"Please take care of your body, too."
But do not miss the other side of this message.
Practical care is not a replacement for God.
Medicine is not our savior.
Physicians are not omnipotent.
Human knowledge has limits.
Even the best treatment cannot guarantee the outcome we desire.
Our ultimate hope is not that we will never experience physical weakness in this fallen world.
Our ultimate hope is Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:23 speaks of believers waiting for the redemption of their bodies.
And Revelation 21:4 points us toward the astonishing promise that God will wipe away every tear and that death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That future hope matters.
Because Christianity does not teach that every believer will enjoy perfect physical health before death.
It promises something greater through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
A final victory over death itself.
A restored creation.
Life with God.
A future in which suffering will not have the last word.
So if you are still waiting for healing, do not confuse waiting with worthlessness.
If you need treatment, do not confuse treatment with unbelief.
If your body is tired, do not confuse exhaustion with spiritual failure.
And if you are praying through tears tonight, remember that the Lord who hears you is the same Jesus who wept at Lazarus's tomb.
He is not indifferent to human sorrow.
But there is an even deeper question beneath all of this.
Have you trusted Jesus only for what He might do to improve your circumstances, or have you entrusted your life to Him as Savior and Lord?
Because the greatest miracle any of us needs is not merely the temporary restoration of a suffering body.
It is reconciliation with the holy God against whom we have sinned.
Sin is not cured by medicine.
Guilt is not erased by human achievement.
And death is not ultimately defeated by better technology.
We need a Redeemer.
And God has given us one.
Jesus Christ lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed.
Through Him, the guilty can be justified.
Through Him, those who repent and believe can receive new life.
And through Him, even the darkest story can become a testimony of grace.
That is why we keep returning to the words:
Not because following Jesus guarantees that every painful chapter disappears immediately.
But because our worst chapter does not have to be our final chapter.
Sin does not have to define us.
Shame does not have to own us.
Suffering does not have to rob us of hope.
And death itself will not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
Maybe you came to this article because you were curious about wine.
Maybe you expected an argument about whether Christians should drink alcohol.
And yes, Scripture makes an important distinction between Paul's limited instruction to Timothy and the drunkenness repeatedly condemned elsewhere, including Ephesians 5:18.

This verse should not be used to promote intoxication or to encourage someone to self-medicate with alcohol. Modern medical decisions require appropriate professional guidance, and wine is not a universal remedy for stomach illness.
But perhaps you discovered something far more personal.
You discovered that a faithful servant of God could experience recurring sickness.
You discovered that an apostle could recommend practical care without abandoning belief in divine healing.
You discovered that the Bible makes room for human weakness without automatically treating it as spiritual defeat.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you are beginning to understand that you do not have to pretend to be invincible to belong to Jesus.
If that truth reached somewhere deep inside you, don't rush past it.
Pray.
Be honest with God.
Ask Him for healing, wisdom, endurance, and the courage to receive appropriate help.
And if you have been blaming yourself for every unanswered prayer, bring that burden before Christ.
Let Scripture correct what fear, shame, or careless teaching may have placed upon your shoulders.
You are not saved by how successfully you hide your weakness. You are saved by the grace of Jesus Christ.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Him, today is an opportunity to turn from sin and trust the Savior who died and rose again.
You do not need to arrive with a polished testimony.
You need to come to Christ.
There may be someone in your family who needs to hear this.
Someone who stopped attending church because they felt judged for being sick.
Someone who thinks God has abandoned them because their prayers for healing have not been answered the way they hoped.
Someone who is quietly ashamed of needing medicine, counseling, rest, or help.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because a message of biblical truth and compassion may reach someone who would never openly admit what they are facing.
And I want to invite you to do something more personal.
If you need your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you in prayer, simply write:
You don't have to share private medical details or explain everything.
Your words may encourage another believer who is still waiting.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where grace is never confused with permission to sin, where repentance is proclaimed, and where struggling people are continually pointed back to Jesus Christ.
Because behind every article, every biblical teaching, every devotional, and every effort to reach another soul is ongoing work that needs faithful support.
If you are already giving faithfully to your local church, please continue to honor that commitment. We do not want you to neglect your congregation or feel pressured to redirect your tithes.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And that is the heart with which we invite you.
Not fear.
Not guilt.
Not the promise that a payment will purchase God's favor.
But grateful participation in work intended to glorify Jesus Christ.
Our desire is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, repent of sin, grow in grace, and follow Christ with greater faithfulness.
You are still welcome here.
You never know whose heart may be reached through something you chose to pass along.
Our mission is to make much of Jesus.
Because one day, the applause of this world will fade.
The things we bought will wear out.
The strength of our bodies will eventually fail.
But the Word of God will stand forever.
And the Gospel of Jesus Christ will remain the only sure hope for sinners who need forgiveness and a world longing for redemption.
So return to Timothy for one final moment.
Picture a young minister, carrying responsibility for God's people while dealing with recurring illness.
And picture an older apostle, writing to him with concern.
Not merely about his doctrine.
Not merely about his leadership.
But about his health.
A little wine.
A troubled stomach.
Frequent infirmities.
A few words that God, in His providence, allowed to remain in Scripture for generations to read.
And perhaps those words are reminding us today that faithfulness is not the absence of weakness.
It is continuing to trust and obey the Lord in the midst of it.
Pray for healing.
Seek wise care.
Receive help without shame.
Reject the lie that every unanswered prayer is proof of God's rejection.
And above everything else, keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because your greatest hope is not that you will never have another difficult day.
Your greatest hope is that the crucified and risen Christ is able to save you, sustain you, and bring you into the fullness of the life He has promised.
Timothy's stomach was still troubling him, but his weakness had not disqualified him from being loved, guided, and used by God. And neither does yours.
